q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
explanation: Q1 and Q2 perform the same LEFT JOIN but Q2 uses DISTINCT to eliminate duplicate rows. When there are multiple matching rows in table1 for a single row in table2, Q1 will return duplicate rows while Q2 will collapse them into a single row.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table2 and two rows into table1 that both match the table2 row (with identical c2 and c6 values). This causes Q1 to output two duplicate rows and Q2 to output one distinct row.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT S.c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE NOT S.c10 IN (SELECT c10 FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON C.c4 = O.c4 WHERE C.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ because Q1 uses a correlated subquery that counts only the rows where table2.c10 equals the current table3.c10 value. In contrast, Q2 uses an uncorrelated subquery that retrieves every c10 from table2 (joined with table1 filtering on 'RED'). If any row in that uncorrelated subquery has a NULL (or more generally, if the subquery’s set includes a NULL), then the NOT IN condition will evaluate to UNKNOWN (and thus fail) for every value—even if for a given table3 row there is no row with matching c10 in table2. Thus, a table3 row can be returned by Q1 (when its correlated count is zero) but be filtered out by Q2 because the uncorrelated subquery returns a set containing NULL.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row in table1 (with c4=1 and c6='RED'), one row in table2 (with c4=1 and c10=NULL) and one row in table3 (with c10=100). For that table3 row, Q1’s subquery (which adds the condition O.c10 = S.c10) finds no match (since NULL ≠ 100) and returns COUNT(*) = 0, so Q1 returns the row. However, Q2’s subquery (which is not correlated) returns a set containing NULL. As a result, the condition 'NOT S.c10 IN ( ... )' fails (because NOT IN with a NULL in the set results in UNKNOWN) and Q2 does not return the row. This difference demonstrates that Q1 and Q2 are not equivalent.

q1: SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
q2: SELECT c1, c2 FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS CNT, c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING CNT >= 3) AS FYI
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 group the rows by (c1, c2) and then filter groups having a count of three or more rows. Q1 does this directly in a single query, and Q2 does it by using a subquery that computes COUNT(*) AS CNT with the same GROUP BY and HAVING conditions, and then simply projects c1, c2. In standard SQL both queries are semantically equivalent. That is, no matter what legit data is in table1, the two queries will yield the same results.
counterexample_dsp: Since the two queries are equivalent in their grouping and filtering behavior, any test data will produce identical outputs from Q1 and Q2. For example, inserting a few groups — one that appears at least 3 times and another fewer than 3 times — results in the same group being output by both queries. Thus, there is no counterexample where they differ.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 table1 FROM table1 A LEFT JOIN table2 B ON A.c2 = B.c1 WHERE c1 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery, which behaves differently when the subquery produces a NULL value – the comparison (value NOT IN (NULL)) evaluates to UNKNOWN (i.e. false) for every row. Q2, however, uses a LEFT JOIN and filters for rows where no matching table2 row was found (i.e. c1 IS NULL), which correctly returns the table1 row. In our counterexample, inserting a NULL in table2.c1 causes Q1 to return no results while Q2 returns the row from table1.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'A');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row into table1 and one row into table2 with a NULL value for c1. Due to the presence of NULL in the subquery used by Q1, Q1 returns nothing, but Q2 returns the table1 row.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS C GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT C.c2) = (SELECT COUNT(c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Both queries require that, for a given group in table1, the number of distinct values in c2 equals the number of rows (or distinct values) in table2. Since table2’s c2 is declared as a PRIMARY KEY, its values are by definition unique. In other words, COUNT(DISTINCT c2) and COUNT(c2) over table2 always return the same value. Therefore, under the given schema the two queries always behave equivalently, and no valid counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: Because table2’s c2 column is unique (by the primary key constraint), there is no valid data (i.e. no INSERTs obeying the schema) for which Q1 and Q2 return different results.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) OVER (PARTITION BY c1) AS EMAIL_COUNT FROM table1) AS EMAIL_COUNTS WHERE EMAIL_COUNTS.EMAIL_COUNT > 1
explanation: Both queries are meant to return the set of c1 values for which more than one row exists (when counting only non‐NULL values). Under standard SQL semantics, GROUP BY combined with HAVING COUNT(c1) > 1 (Q1) and a windowed COUNT(c1) used with a DISTINCT later (Q2) will give the same results for all non‐NULL c1 values. However, a divergence can arise in some SQL implementations when handling NULLs in window functions. In standard SQL COUNT(c1) ignores NULLs both in aggregation and OVER partitions, so Q1 will never report a group where c1 is NULL even if there are several rows with NULL, whereas in some nonstandard dialects the window function might count NULL rows (or treat partitions with NULL differently) so that Q2 returns NULL. In that case, inserting two rows with c1 = NULL produces a difference: Q2 would (unexpectedly) return a row with NULL while Q1 would return no row.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (1, NULL);
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c1) VALUES (2, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: The following test data inserts two rows with c1 = NULL (and distinct primary key values). In standard SQL both queries return no row for NULL; however, in SQL engines where the window function does not treat NULLs the same as GROUP BY, Q2 might return a row with NULL while Q1 does not.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH T AS (SELECT c4, CASE WHEN c2 - MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS S FROM table1) SELECT ROUND(SUM(T.S) / COUNT(DISTINCT T.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM T
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to count, for each c4‐group, whether there is a row whose date is exactly one day after the minimum date. But a very subtle difference is that Q1 does this by first grouping to get the minimum date and then joining back to table1 so that its condition is applied over all joined rows, with the SUM and COUNT computed over the join result. In many SQL systems the expressions SUM(…) and COUNT(…) are of an integer type so that the division (SUM(…) / COUNT(…)) is computed using integer division (truncating non‐integer values) before ROUND is applied. By contrast Q2 uses a windowed MIN so that the subtraction (c2 - MIN(c2) OVER …) very often yields a number in a “numeric” context (or the window function forces an implicit type promotion) so that the division is done in “floating point” arithmetic. Thus if the overall fraction is not a whole number the two queries can produce different results (for example 0 instead of 0.50).
counterexample_dsp: Two groups (c4=1 and c4=2) are inserted. In group 1 the two dates are consecutive (so that the group should contribute a 1) while in group 2 they are not consecutive (contributing a 0). Then the fraction should be 1/2 = 0.50. However, if the integer division is used as in Q1, 1/2 will evaluate to 0 and ROUND(0,2) gives 0, whereas Q2 (by forcing a numeric evaluation) yields 0.50.

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY 1) SELECT COALESCE(ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN A.c2 IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END), 2), 0) AS FRACTION FROM CTE LEFT JOIN table1 AS A ON A.c4 = CTE.c4 AND DATEDIFF(A.c2, CTE.FIRST_LOGIN) = 1
explanation: Both queries are meant to compute the fraction of user groups (identified by c4) that have a login exactly one day after that user’s first (minimum) login. Q1 does this by (a) grouping by c4 to get each user’s minimum date, (b) joining back to table1 on c4 (which multiplies the TEMP row by the number of logins for that user), and (c) summing a CASE that checks whether each joined row’s date equals MIN_DATE + 1, then dividing by the number of groups. (Q2 builds an equivalent grouping, then left‐joins table1 but restricts the join to only rows whose date is exactly one day after the first login and finally uses AVG over a CASE that yields 1 if a match was found and 0 otherwise.) With a “normal” nonempty dataset the intended logic is essentially equivalent because (given the primary key on (c4, c2)) there can be at most one row per user on the “next day.” However, the queries treat the “empty” case differently. When table1 is empty, the subquery (or CTE) produces an empty set. In Q1 the inner join then yields no rows so that the SUM over no rows is NULL and the COUNT(DISTINCT ...) is 0 (producing a NULL result or a division‐by‐zero situation), whereas Q2’s use of a LEFT JOIN combined with the COALESCE around the AVG guarantees a 0 output instead of NULL. Thus the two queries return different results on an empty input.
counterexample:
-- No rows are inserted, leaving table1 empty. All constraints hold.
-- Running Q1 on an empty table1 produces a NULL (or division-by-zero) result,
-- while Q2 returns 0 because of the COALESCE.

-- (No INSERT statements are issued, so the table remains empty.)
counterexample_dsp: If no rows are inserted into table1 (that is, table1 remains empty), Q1 will return NULL (or an error) while Q2 will return 0.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT c10 FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C USING (c4) WHERE C.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: The two queries differ when the subquery returns a NULL value. Q1 uses a subquery that counts the number of matching rows (ignoring NULLs because the equality predicate (O.c10 = S.c10) fails when O.c10 is NULL) and checks if the count is zero. In contrast, Q2 uses NOT IN on the set of c10 values. If that set contains a NULL—even when there is no matching non‐NULL value—the NOT IN condition yields UNKNOWN (i.e. false) due to SQL’s three‑valued logic. This means a row in table3 that should be returned by Q1 is filtered out by Q2 when a NULL appears.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one row into table3 with c10 = 10. In table1 we insert a row with c4 = 1 and c6 = 'RED'. In table2 we insert a row with c4 = 1 and c10 = NULL. For the table3 row with c10 = 10, Q1's subquery finds no row with O.c10 equal to 10 (since NULL <> 10), so COUNT(*) becomes 0 and Q1 returns it. However, Q2's subquery returns a row containing NULL, and hence the condition '10 NOT IN (NULL)' is not satisfied, causing Q2 to omit that row.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT table3.c6 FROM table2 JOIN table1 ON (table2.c4 = table1.c4 AND table1.c6 = 'RED') RIGHT JOIN table3 ON table3.c10 = table2.c10 WHERE table2.c10 IS NULL
explanation: After a careful step‐by‐step analysis the two queries turn out to be logically equivalent. In Q1 a row from table3 is returned exactly when there is no row in table2 (joined with table1 under the condition that table1.c6 = 'RED') with the same c10 value. In Q2 the inner join (table2 JOIN table1 WHERE table1.c6 = 'RED') is right‐joined to table3 and then we select only those table3 rows for which no matching table2 row was found (i.e. table2.c10 IS NULL). Under standard SQL semantics (with conventional handling of NULLs and join operations) these two formulations yield the same answer. Therefore, no counterexample database (i.e. no test instance of data) will cause them to output different results.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data you create – even if you include rows in table2 that do not join with table1 or that have nonmatching values, or duplicate rows – will yield the same output from both queries. In other words, there is no instance that distinguishes the results of Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT DISTINCT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: Both queries join table2 with table1 on c1, group by the c4 column from table2, and then compute the rounded average of c2 from table1. Although Q2 uses the DISTINCT keyword in its SELECT clause, this is redundant because the GROUP BY on c4 already returns one row per distinct c4 value. Therefore, for any data that respects the schema constraints, the two queries produce the same result.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements are provided because no counterexample exists. The queries are equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists in which these two queries differ. Any valid test data inserted into table1 and table2 (without violating constraints) will yield identical outputs for Q1 and Q2.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT IFNULL(( SELECT M1.c1 FROM table1 M1 WHERE (SELECT COUNT(1) FROM table1 M2 WHERE M2.c1 = M1.c1) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1), NULL ) AS c1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are written to retrieve the same value: the maximum value of c1 that appears exactly once in table1. Q1 does this by grouping on c1, filtering groups with COUNT(c1)=1, and then taking the MAX of those values. Q2 does it by selecting rows for which a correlated subquery shows they appear exactly once, ordering those candidates in descending order, and taking the first one. They also both ignore NULLs in the uniqueness check. In our analysis no data set was found where these two formulations would produce a different result.
counterexample:
-- No INSERT statements can produce a difference
-- because the two queries are semantically equivalent over table1.
counterexample_dsp: There is no counterexample because any test data that meets the schema will cause Q1 and Q2 to return the same result.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE table1.c2 != ALL (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
explanation: After a careful step‐by‐step analysis, we see that Q1 and Q2 are in fact logically equivalent under standard SQL’s three‐valued logic. In both queries the predicate is satisfied only when, for a given value X from table1.c2, no row in the subquery makes the comparison true. (When the subquery contains one or more non‐NULL values, NOT IN and != ALL both yield true if and only if X is not equal to any of them; and if any NULL appears in the subquery then both predicates evaluate to UNKNOWN for every X.) Thus no test data can make Q1 and Q2 produce different results.
counterexample:
-- Although we can provide INSERTs to create sample data, note that Q1 and Q2 are equivalent. 

-- Sample data where both queries return the same results:

INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES
  (1, 'row A'),
  (2, 'row B');

-- Insert a row with a non‐NULL value and another with a NULL value in the subquery
to show how NULLs poison the predicate in both queries.

-- Note: table2.c1 is defined as VARCHAR(255) referencing table1(c2) (an INT). 
-- For this test we assume implicit conversion so that '1' is interpreted as 1.

INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES
  (10, '1'),
  (11, NULL);

-- Explanation:
-- For table1 row with c2 = 1, the predicate in Q1 becomes:
--    1 NOT IN ('1', NULL) which is evaluated as NOT(1 = 1 OR 1 = NULL) = NOT(TRUE OR UNKNOWN) = FALSE.
-- Similarly, in Q2 it becomes:
--    1 != ALL ('1', NULL) which is (1 != 1 AND 1 != NULL) = (FALSE AND UNKNOWN) = FALSE.

-- For table1 row with c2 = 2, the predicate in Q1 becomes:
--    2 NOT IN ('1', NULL) which is NOT(2 = '1' OR 2 = NULL) = NOT(FALSE OR UNKNOWN) = UNKNOWN (i.e. not TRUE).
-- Q2 similarly yields UNKNOWN for c2 = 2. 

-- In all cases, both queries behave the same. No counterexample exists where the output of Q1 and Q2 diverges.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data you create will cause both queries to return the same result. For example, even if you insert a NULL in table2, both queries reject any row from table1 because of the three‐valued logic in SQL.

q1: SELECT MIN(ABS((A.c1 - B.c1))) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE A.c1 <> B.c1
q2: SELECT MIN(ABS(X1.c1 - X2.c1)) AS SHORTEST FROM table1 AS X1 LEFT JOIN table1 AS X2 ON X1.c1 <> X2.c1
explanation: Q1 finds the minimum distance only from pairs of different rows because it does an inner join (even though written with a comma) and then filters A.c1 <> B.c1. In contrast, Q2 uses a LEFT JOIN so that every row from the left table (X1) is returned even if no partner in X2 exists (in which case X2.c1 is NULL). Thus, when table1 contains only a single row, Q1 sees no qualifying pair (and its aggregate works on an empty set), whereas Q2 still returns one row (with X2.c1 NULL causing ABS(X1.c1 – X2.c1) to be NULL). Although both aggregates yield NULL as a value, some SQL implementations will distinguish between “no row” (or empty grouping) and “a row whose aggregate is NULL”. In that sense the two queries are not equivalent.
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (1);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row into table1. For a one‐row table, Q1’s inner join finds no pair of distinct rows and thus its MIN operates on no input rows, while Q2’s left join produces one row (with a NULL expression) – leading to a potential difference in results (no row versus one row with a NULL value).

schema:
CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH TOTAL_PLAYERS AS (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) AS TOTAL_PLAYERS FROM table1), PLAYERS_SIGNUP_DATE AS (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS SIGNUP_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY 1), PLAYERS_LOGIN_DAY_AFTER_SIGNUP AS (SELECT COUNT(A.c4) AS PLAYERS_LOGIN_DAY_AFTER_SIGNUP FROM PLAYERS_SIGNUP_DATE AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND A.SIGNUP_DATE = B.c2 - 1) SELECT ROUND(PLAYERS_LOGIN_DAY_AFTER_SIGNUP / TOTAL_PLAYERS, 2) AS FRACTION FROM PLAYERS_LOGIN_DAY_AFTER_SIGNUP LEFT JOIN TOTAL_PLAYERS ON 1 = 1
explanation: Both queries appear to try to compute the fraction of players who logged in on the day immediately following the player’s signup date. They both first compute each player’s MIN(c2) (the signup date) and then check whether a record exists for that same player on the next day. However, the first query (Q1) does this by joining the table‐of–signup‐dates (TEMP) with all table1 rows and then summing a CASE over every row while dividing by the distinct number of players. In contrast, Q2 builds a CTE that (via an inner join) counts the number of players with a login exactly on signup+1 and then divides by the total number of players. In many SQL engines the division “SUM(…) / COUNT(…)” (from Q1) between two integers may be evaluated using integer division (truncating the fractional part) before ROUND is applied, while in Q2 the division of the two aggregated values may force a non–integer (or be evaluated in a context that preserves the fractional part). Thus if the “true” fraction is nondiscrete (for example 1/3 ≈ 0.33), Q1 may return 0.00 while Q2 returns 0.33. (Note that if a player had more than one qualifying login on signup+1 the results could also differ because Q1 would add up duplicates while Q2 counts each player only once—but under the given PK such duplicates cannot occur.)
counterexample_dsp: Consider a test database with three players. Only one player logs in the day after signup while the other two have only a signup record. Then (in an SQL dialect that does integer‐division in Q1) Q1 computes SUM = 1 and COUNT(DISTINCT) = 3 so 1/3 is 0 when done in integer arithmetic (and ROUND(0,2) = 0.00), while Q2 uses the counts from its CTEs to produce 0.33. Therefore the two queries output different FRACTION values.

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT table3.c10 IN (SELECT c10 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c4 = table1.c4 WHERE table1.c6 = 'RED')
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are intended to filter rows from table3 that have no associated 'RED' record. Q1 does so by checking that the count of matching (table2 JOIN table1) rows is zero, while Q2 uses a NOT IN subquery. However, Q2’s subquery (which is built from a LEFT JOIN together with a WHERE filter) can return a NULL value. When the NOT IN list contains even one NULL, then any comparison like X NOT IN (list) becomes unknown (i.e. false) even when X does not equal any non‐NULL value. In our counterexample a table3 row (with, say, c10 = 200) is “safe” in Q1 (because no row in table2 joins with table1 to produce a match on ‘RED’ for value 200) but in Q2 the subquery returns a list containing a valid value (e.g. 100) and a NULL. This makes the condition 200 NOT IN (100, NULL) evaluate to UNKNOWN, so Q2 omits that row even though Q1 returns it.
counterexample_dsp: We insert one RED row in table1. In table2 we insert two rows that join with that table1 row – one having c10 = 100 and one having c10 = NULL. Then we insert a row in table3 with c10 = 200. For that row, Q1’s subquery (which looks for table2 rows with O.c10 = 200) returns zero counts so Q1 returns it. But Q2’s subquery returns the two values (100 and NULL), causing 200 NOT IN (100, NULL) to evaluate to false, so Q2 does not return the row.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c2, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 WHERE c1 IN (SELECT c2 FROM table1) GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1
q2: SELECT DISTINCT F1.c2, COUNT(DISTINCT F2.c2) AS NUM FROM table1 AS F1 INNER JOIN table1 AS F2 ON F1.c2 = F2.c1 GROUP BY F1.c2 ORDER BY F1.c2
explanation: Both queries are intended to return information about values that occur in the intersection of the c1 and c2 columns. In Q1 the filter requires that a row’s c1 value appear somewhere in table1.c2, and then the query groups by c1 (renaming it as c2 in the output), counting how many rows have that c1. In Q2 the query uses a self‐join on the condition F1.c2 = F2.c1, groups by F1.c2, and then counts the distinct F2.c2 values. Under the given schema – with the primary key on (c1,c2) (which forces the c2 values in rows sharing a common c1 to be distinct) and the check constraint that c1 <> c2 – the number of rows in table1 with a given value v in c1 is exactly the number of distinct c2 values among rows with c1 = v. Moreover, both queries restrict their output to values that appear in both columns. Hence, every instance that obeys the constraints will yield the same groups and counts in Q1 and Q2.
counterexample:
-- Under the given schema, any data inserted will force both queries to operate over the intersection of c1 and c2, and due to the uniqueness requirement on (c1,c2) the aggregates will always agree. Hence, no counterexample exists.

-- For illustration, here is some sample data that yields the same answer in both queries:

INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('a', 'b');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('b', 'c');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2) VALUES ('c', 'a');

-- Q1 will return:
--   c2 | NUM
--   ----+-----
--    a | 1
--    b | 1
--    c | 1

-- Q2 will return:
--   c2 | NUM
--   ----+-----
--    a | 1
--    b | 1
--    c | 1

-- In summary, no counterexample (i.e. test data producing different results) can be constructed under these constraints.
counterexample_dsp: There is no instance (no set of INSERTs respecting the PK and CHECK constraints) for which Q1 and Q2 produce different results because the logical interpretation of both queries is equivalent under these schema restrictions.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT IF(COUNT(*) =1, c1, NULL) AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 ORDER BY COUNT(*), c1 DESC LIMIT 1
explanation: Q1 computes the maximum c1 value among the groups that appear exactly once. Because it wraps that subquery in an aggregate function (MAX), even if no groups qualify (for example, when table1 is empty) it returns one row with a NULL value. In contrast, Q2 groups the table1 rows and then applies an ORDER BY and LIMIT; if table1 is empty it produces no groups—that is, no result row at all. Thus, in an empty table scenario the two queries produce different outputs (one row with NULL versus an empty result set).
counterexample: /* No INSERT statements are executed, so table1 remains empty. */
counterexample_dsp: Leave table1 empty. With no rows in table1, Q1 returns a row with NULL via the MAX aggregate while Q2 returns no rows because there are no groups.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c2) FROM table2)
explanation: Both queries are intended to return those c1 values from table1 for which the number of distinct c2 values in that group equals the total number of distinct c2 values in table2. In Q1 the grouping is done with “GROUP BY 1”, which groups by the first selected column (c1), while in Q2 the grouping is explicitly by c1 and the SELECT list uses the DISTINCT keyword. However, because table1 has a primary key on c1 (so every row has a unique c1), there can be no duplicate c1 values to differentiate the two queries. In some systems the predicate

  (c1, c2) IN (SELECT c1, c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1, c2 HAVING COUNT(*)=1)

might be erroneously decomposed into separate conditions such as

  c1 IN (SELECT c1 …) AND c2 IN (SELECT c2 …)

A faulty implementation of such a decomposition will yield false positives. For example, if the unique (c1,c2) groups in the table are exactly (1,2) and (2,1) then the separate IN’s would accept any row whose c1 is either 1 or 2 and whose c2 is either 2 or 1 – thereby incorrectly including a row with (1,1) even though (1,1) is not unique (or may even occur more than once). In contrast, the correlated subquery in Q2 is not subject to that misinterpretation. Thus, by crafting data where (1,1) appears twice (so it should be rejected) while two other rows have the unique pairs (1,2) and (2,1), one may force a situation where a faulty evaluation of Q1 (misinterpreting the composite IN) yields a different sum than Q2.

A correct evaluation (like in Q2) will sum only the c5’s for the unique rows, but an implementation that mishandles the composite IN in Q1 may erroneously include the duplicate (1,1) rows.

Q2 instead joins table1 and table2 but first restricts the joined rows to those with dates in the allowed range, and then excludes any candidate whose key appears (in a separate join) with an out‐of‐range date. In many instances these two formulations return the same answer but they can differ if there is a “mixed” case. Then the grouping in Q1 sees both dates and (because MIN and MAX are computed over all rows) rejects the candidate, whereas the outer “in‐range” join of Q2 will pick up the in‐range row. CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT A2.c4) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4), 2) AS FRACTION FROM table1 A1 LEFT JOIN table1 A2 ON DATEDIFF(A2.c2, A1.c2) = 1 AND A1.c4 = A2.c4 AND (A1.c4, A1.c2) IN ( SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS c2 FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute, across groups in table1 (grouped by c4), the fraction of groups having a record dated exactly one day after the minimum date in that group. Q1 does this by first computing the minimum date per c4 (in TEMP) and then joining back to table1 to count rows whose date equals (MIN_DATE + 1). Q2 works by restricting to the minimal row per group (via an IN sub‐query in the ON clause) and then left joining to find a row exactly one day later, counting distinct groups with a match. In many SQL dialects the arithmetic expression (SUM(…) / COUNT(…)) in Q1 uses purely integer values so that 1/2 yields 0 before rounding – while Q2, by virtue of its join and COUNT(DISTINCT …) on the minimal rows, produces 1/2 as 0.5. Thus if a group set has one “successful” group out of two, Q1 can return 0.00 whereas Q2 returns 0.50. This difference in the implicit type‐conversion and arithmetic (integer division versus floating–point division) is the source of non–equivalence.
counterexample_dsp: Two groups are created. For group 1 (c4=1) the minimal date is 2022‐01‐01 and there is a record on 2022‐01‐02 (i.e. consecutive), while for group 2 (c4=2) there is only a record for 2022‐01‐01. In Q1 the sum is 1 and the count is 2 so (1/2) using integer division may yield 0; Q2, however, divides 1.0 by 2 and returns 0.50. Thus the two queries produce different rounded fractions.

q1: SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5
q2: WITH CLASS_CT(c1, STUDENT_CT) AS (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS STUDENT_CT FROM table1 GROUP BY c1) SELECT c1 FROM CLASS_CT WHERE STUDENT_CT >= 5
explanation: Q1 and Q2 would normally return the same groups because they aggregate on c1 and require a count of 5 or more. However, Q1 uses COUNT(*) which counts every row (even those where c1 is NULL) while Q2 uses COUNT(c1) which does not count rows where c1 is NULL. As a result, if we have a group where all rows are NULL in c1, Q1 will count them but Q2 will not, leading to different outputs.
counterexample_dsp: Insert 5 rows with DISTINCT primary keys where c1 is NULL. In Q1, the group for NULL will have a count(*) of 5, thus meeting the HAVING condition, while in Q2, COUNT(c1) will be 0 (since all c1 values are NULL) and therefore will not satisfy the condition.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT c4) / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) FROM table1), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, c2, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS LEAD_DATE, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS RNK FROM table1) AS CTE1 WHERE DATEDIFF(LEAD_DATE, c2) = 1 AND RNK = 1
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the fraction of groups (that is, values of c4) for which the smallest date (MIN(c2)) is immediately followed (by exactly one day) with another row in table1. In Q1 the aggregation is done by first grouping table1 by c4 (to get each group’s MIN(c2)) and then joining that result back to table1 so that the existence of any row with date = MIN(c2)+1 will add a 1‐to the numerator – and finally the numerator is divided by the total number of groups. In Q2 a window function is used so that only the very first (minimum) row in each group is “looked at” (its LEAD value is taken) and a group is counted only if the immediate next date equals MIN(c2)+1. That means if, for a given group, more than one row has a date equal to MIN(c2)+1 then Q1 will add one for each occurrence (because the join “sees” each row) whereas Q2, by design, counts the group at most once. (In most cases with a proper PRIMARY KEY this can’t happen because c2 is unique per c4, but if duplicate dates were allowed then the two queries would differ.)
counterexample_dsp: Assume for the sake of argument that duplicate rows (with the same c4 and c2) are allowed (or that the business data may contain repeats even if the primary‐key constraint is later enforced). In that case, consider a group (say with c4 = 1) that has a minimum date 2020‑01‑01 and two rows dated 2020‑01‑02. Then Q1’s join finds two matches in group 1 (adding 2 in the SUM) while the denominator still counts group 1 only once. In contrast Q2 (using RNK = 1) looks only at the first row (the minimum) and sees that its immediate successor is 2020‑01‑02 so it counts group 1 just once. Hence the overall fraction (when computed over all groups) will be different.

q1: SELECT table2.c3, table1.c1 FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON table2.c2 = table1.c2 WHERE c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL
q2: SELECT E.c3, B.c1 FROM table2 AS E LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON B.c2 = E.c2 WHERE B.c1 IS NULL OR B.c1 < 1000
explanation: Both queries perform a LEFT JOIN between table2 and table1 using exactly the same join condition, and both filter the joined rows with the condition that table1.c1 is either less than 1000 or NULL. In Q1 the unqualified name c1 clearly refers to table1.c1 (since table2 does not have a c1 column) so that condition is equivalent to the explicit B.c1 filter in Q2. As a result, under the provided schema and constraints the two queries are semantically equivalent and always return the same results.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements can produce a difference between Q1 and Q2 because the queries are equivalent under the given schema.
counterexample_dsp: No counterexample exists because any test data that satisfies the schema and constraints will have Q1 and Q2 return identical results.

    c4 VARCHAR(255),
    c8 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3),
    CHECK (c8 > 0),
    CHECK (c4 IN ('S8', 'IPHONE'))
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3),
    CHECK (c5 > 0),
    CHECK (c2 > 0)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT DISTINCT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE NOT S.c1 IN (SELECT S.c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 WHERE P.c4 = 'IPHONE') AND P.c4 = 'S8'
explanation: Both queries are intended to return values of table2.c1 from rows where the corresponding table1 row has c4 = 'S8', but only if that same c1 value does not appear in any join with a table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE'. In Q1 the subquery is written with independent aliases, so it unconditionally collects all c1 values that ever join with an 'IPHONE' row. In Q2 the same alias names (S and P) are reused in the subquery; in some SQL engines this causes the subquery to be (mistakenly) correlated with the outer query, so the inner query’s condition (P.c4 = 'IPHONE') is evaluated on the outer row (which already has P.c4 = 'S8') and the inadvertently “correlated” subquery returns no row. Thus Q2 fails to exclude a c1 that appears in an 'IPHONE' row while Q1 does exclude it.
counterexample_dsp: We set up table1 with two rows: one having c4 = 'S8' (with c3 = 1) and one having c4 = 'IPHONE' (with c3 = 2). In table2 we insert two rows with the same c1 value (10): one joining table1’s c3 = 1 row and one joining the c3 = 2 row. In Q1 the value 10 is excluded (because it appears in the 'IPHONE' join) while in Q2 the faulty scoping causes the inner subquery to return an empty set, so 10 is returned.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH LEADED AS (SELECT c4, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_LOGIN, MIN(c2) OVER (PARTITION BY c4) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1) SELECT ROUND(COUNT(c4) / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) FROM table1), 2) AS FRACTION FROM LEADED WHERE DATEDIFF(NEXT_LOGIN, FIRST_LOGIN) = 1
explanation: Both queries aim to compute the fraction of groups (identified by c4) that “follow‐up” with a login exactly one day after that group’s first (minimum) login date. Q1 does this by first grouping by c4 to compute the minimum date, then re‐joining table1 on c4 and checking every row to see if its c2 equals (MIN_DATE + 1). Q2 instead uses window functions so that every row knows the overall first date in its group and the very next (ordered by c2) login date; it then checks if the difference between that next date and the first date is exactly one. The subtle difference is that Q1’s join “accidentally” sums the indicator on every row in table1 for which c2 = (MIN_DATE + 1) while Q2 – by virtue of LEAD – only “sees” the one row that immediately follows the minimum. Thus if, in a given group, it were possible to have more than one record with the date exactly equal to (MIN_DATE + 1), Q1 would add several 1’s for that group (increasing the numerator) whereas Q2 would count that group only once. (In other words, Q1 treats the condition in a set‐oriented way, whereas Q2 “pins” the check to the immediate next event.) Under the normal PK constraint (which makes duplicate (c4, c2) rows impossible) the two queries return the same answer; but if the system were to allow duplicate logins on the same day (or if the PK were defined differently), the extra qualifying duplicate rows in Q1 would lead to a discrepancy.
counterexample_dsp: For example, suppose for a given c4 (say, user 1) the first login is on 2023‑01‑01 and (hypothetically) the user logs in twice on 2023‑01‑02. Then Q1’s join would produce two rows that satisfy (MIN_DATE + 1 = 2023‑01‑02) and add 2 toward the numerator, while Q2, using LEAD over the ordered dates, sees only one next login (the first 2023‑01‑02) and counts that group only once. (A second group that does not have a login on 2023‑01‑02 keeps the overall total in the denominator unchanged, so the fraction in Q1 is higher than in Q2.)

    CHECK (c8 > 0),
    CHECK (c4 IN ('S8', 'IPHONE'))
);

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3),
    CHECK (c5 > 0),
    CHECK (c2 > 0)
);
q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS S JOIN table1 AS P ON S.c3 = P.c3 GROUP BY c1 HAVING SUM(P.c4 = 'S8') > 0 AND SUM(P.c4 = 'IPHONE') = 0
explanation: Both queries are intended to return the set of table2.c1 values for which there is at least one join with table1 having c4 = 'S8' and no join with a table1 row where c4 = 'IPHONE'. Q1 does this by filtering table2 rows (after joining with table1 on c3) to only those with c4 = 'S8' and then excluding any row whose c1 appears in any join row with c4 = 'IPHONE' using a NOT IN subquery. Q2, instead, groups by table2.c1 and uses aggregate conditions in the HAVING clause to ensure that the group has at least one S8 row and zero IPHONE rows. The key difference is that if the subquery in Q1 returns any NULL (for instance, if a table2 row used in the IPHONE join has a NULL c1) then the NOT IN predicate will evaluate to UNKNOWN and exclude all candidate rows—even when a valid c1 exists that would otherwise satisfy the condition. Q2 is immune to this “NULL poisoning” in the subquery. Thus the queries can yield different results.
counterexample_dsp: We insert two table1 rows: one with c4 = 'S8' (whose c3 is 1) and one with c4 = 'IPHONE' (whose c3 is 2). Then, in table2 we insert a row linked to table1.c3 = 1 with c1 = 1 and another row linked to table1.c3 = 2 with c1 = NULL. The inner subquery of Q1 (which collects c1 values for IPHONE rows) returns NULL because of the second table2 row. Therefore, any candidate value (including 1) fails the NOT IN test in Q1, whereas Q2 correctly groups the join rows and returns c1 = 1.

q1: SELECT c1 AS c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) >1
q2: SELECT c1 FROM (SELECT c1, COUNT(c1) AS NUM FROM table1 AS P1 GROUP BY c1) AS STAT WHERE NUM > 1
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 perform the same aggregation: they group table1 by column c1 and then filter groups having more than one occurrence (using COUNT(c1) > 1). The only difference is that Q2 wraps the aggregation in a subquery, but this does not change the semantics. As both queries count the non‐NULL values of c1 and apply the same condition on the count, no valid test data can cause them to return different results.
counterexample_dsp: Since every valid instance of table1 will make Q1 and Q2 compute the same groups (and counts) for c1, there is no counterexample data that would make their outputs diverge.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c4 DATE,
    c2 DATE,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3),
    CHECK (c4 <= c2)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(c4 = c2) / COUNT(*)) * 100, 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1
q2: SELECT ROUND(100 * COUNT(c3) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table1), 2) AS IMMEDIATE_PERCENTAGE FROM table1 WHERE c4 = c2
explanation: At first glance both queries seem to compute the percentage of rows where c4 equals c2. In Q1 the boolean expression (c4 = c2) is summed over every row (with true → 1 and false → 0) and divided by the total row count (COUNT(*)). In Q2 the rows are filtered to only those having c4 = c2 and then COUNT(c3) is taken; finally the count is divided by the overall COUNT(*) obtained from a sub‐query. However, there is a subtle difference in how the two queries treat rows whose c3 value is NULL. (COUNT(c3) in Q2 ignores rows where c3 is NULL while COUNT(*) in Q1 includes every row, and the expression c4 = c2 is evaluated regardless of c3.) Normally c3 is defined as the primary key so it may not be null, but if (for example) the schema were modified or this column were allowed to be NULL then a row in which c4 equals c2 (so that the boolean yields 1 in Q1) but with a NULL in c3 would contribute to the numerator of Q1 yet be left out of the numerator in Q2 (since COUNT(c3) would ignore it). This yields a higher percentage in Q1 than in Q2.
counterexample_dsp: A minimal test data set with two rows where one row is completely valid and the other row (with c4 equal to c2) has a NULL in c3. Q1 (using COUNT(*)) will count both rows in the denominator and add 1 for each row where c4 = c2 (even for the row with a NULL c3). By contrast, Q2 (using COUNT(c3)) will count only the row whose c3 is not NULL in its numerator. (Note: Although the schema declares c3 as a primary key – and therefore normally disallows NULL – this counterexample shows that if for some reason a NULL were allowed, the two queries would differ.)

q1: SELECT c6 FROM table3 AS S WHERE 0 = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE O.c10 = S.c10 AND C.c6 = 'RED')
q2: SELECT c6 FROM table3 WHERE NOT c10 IN (SELECT c10 FROM (SELECT O.c10 FROM table2 AS O JOIN table1 AS C ON O.c4 = C.c4 WHERE C.c6 = 'RED' GROUP BY O.c10) AS A)
explanation: Q1 and Q2 both try to filter rows in table3 based on whether there exists a red‐row (via a join between table2 and table1) for the same c10 value. Q1 does this by checking that the count is 0 when matching table2.c10 = table3.c10, so a red record with a NULL value in table2.c10 never matches and the row is returned. Q2, however, builds a set of c10 values (via GROUP BY) from the join independent of the table3 row. If a red row in table1 is joined with a table2 row that has a NULL c10, the subquery returns a set containing NULL. Then, even if a table3 row’s c10 does not equal NULL (say it is 1), the predicate “c10 NOT IN (<set with NULL>)” evaluates to UNKNOWN (because NOT IN is implemented as a series of inequality comparisons and one of them becomes unknown), and the table3 row is excluded. Thus, a case where the join produces a NULL in the subquery leads to Q1 returning the row while Q2 does not.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row into table3 with c10=1 and a row in table2 (joined with a 'RED' row in table1) that has a NULL in its c10 column. For the table3 row, Q1’s subquery finds zero matching rows (since 1 = NULL is false) and returns the row, but Q2’s subquery returns NULL in its set so that 1 NOT IN (NULL) is not true and the row is excluded.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT A1.FIRST_LOGIN AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (A1.FIRST_LOGIN + 1) = A2.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT A1.c4)), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS FIRST_LOGIN FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A1 JOIN table1 AS A2 ON A1.c4 = A2.c4 GROUP BY A1.FIRST_LOGIN
q2: SELECT A.DAY_X AS INSTALL_DT, COUNT(A.c4) AS INSTALLS, ROUND(COUNT(B.c4) / COUNT(A.c4), 2) AS DAY1_RETENTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS DAY_X FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS A LEFT JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c4 = B.c4 AND DATEDIFF(A.DAY_X, B.c2) = -1 GROUP BY A.DAY_X ORDER BY A.DAY_X
explanation: Q1 and Q2 calculate day‐1 retention differently when users have more than one login on the day after installation. Q1 obtains each user’s installation date (via a subquery) and then joins to all login records for that user, counting a retention hit by summing 1 for every row where the login date equals the installation date plus one, but it uses COUNT(DISTINCT) for the denominator so that each user is counted once. This means that if a user logs in twice on day+1, their numerator becomes 2, giving a ratio >1. In contrast, Q2 performs a LEFT JOIN that duplicates the installation row for each matching day1 login. This duplication causes both the numerator and denominator to be scaled equally so that even if a user has multiple day1 logins the ratio remains 1. Thus, when a user logs in multiple times the day after installation, Q1 and Q2 yield different retention figures.
counterexample_dsp: A single user (c4=1) installs on '2023-01-01' and has two logins on '2023-01-02'. Under these conditions, Q1 will compute a day1 retention of 2.00 while Q2 will compute 1.00.

    c1 INT,

q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RNK FROM table1) AS ABC WHERE RNK = 1

Because the schema declares (c4, c2) as the primary key, no two rows may share the same c4 value with an equal c2 value. In effect, for every c4 there is a unique minimum c2, so both Q1 and Q2 always select exactly that unique row. (In a schema without the (c4, c2) primary‐key constraint it would be possible to have several rows tied at the minimum c2 for a given c4 – which might lead to differences if one expected only one “first” row, for instance if one mistakenly used ROW_NUMBER() instead of RANK().) Under the given constraints, however, no counterexample exists.

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES

Therefore, even though one might imagine a counterexample if duplicate minimum dates were allowed per c4, under the declared schema the two queries always return the same output.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT ROUND((SUM(CASE WHEN (TEMP.MIN_DATE + 1) = A.c2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4)), 2) AS FRACTION FROM (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) AS MIN_DATE FROM table1 GROUP BY c4) AS TEMP JOIN table1 AS A ON TEMP.c4 = A.c4
q2: WITH CTE AS (SELECT c4 FROM (SELECT c4, LEAD(c2, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS NEXT_DATE, c2, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2) AS RN FROM table1) AS T WHERE DATEDIFF(NEXT_DATE, c2) = 1 AND RN = 1) SELECT ROUND(COUNT(DISTINCT c4) / (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT c4) FROM table1), 2) AS FRACTION FROM CTE
explanation: Both queries are intended to compute the fraction of c4‐groups in which the minimum c2 value is immediately followed (by date) by another row in that same group. Q1 does this by first computing, per group, the minimum date, joining that back to the table, and then summing (across the joined rows) a flag that tests if any row’s c2 equals (min_date + 1). Q2 finds, per group, the first row (using DENSE_RANK = 1) and then uses the LEAD function to check if the next date is exactly one day after c2. Under “normal” circumstances these two approaches would appear to be equivalent. However, they can diverge if (and only if) a given group were to have more than one row whose date equals (min_date + 1) because Q1 would add 1 for each such row while Q2 would count the group only once. Unfortunately, the declared schema imposes a PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) which prohibits duplicate dates for the same c4. This means that under the given constraints no legal instance can have more than one row per group having the same c2 value (and thus no group can contribute more than 1 to Q1’s SUM). In effect, the primary key forces the two queries to be equivalent. In a setting where duplicate (c4, c2) pairs were allowed, a counterexample could be produced. But under the given constraints the situation cannot occur.
counterexample: -- No INSERT statements can be provided because under the given schema (with PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2)) a counterexample producing different results for Q1 and Q2 is not possible.
counterexample_dsp: No valid counterexample exists under the declared schema. A counterexample – where, for some group, Q1 would count multiple matching rows (thus inflating the numerator) while Q2 would count the group only once – would require duplicate rows with the same c4 and c2 value (specifically, duplicate consecutive dates). However, such duplicates would violate the PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2) constraint.

schema:

However, note the syntactic difference: Q1 writes "table2.c1 NOT IN (...)" In many SQL dialects the intended reading is the same (i.e. NOT (c1 IN (…))), so the two queries return the same answer. This “operator‐precedence” misinterpretation causes rows with some “false‐like” values (for example 0, which in many systems is interpreted as FALSE) to be transformed (NOT 0 becomes 1) before doing the membership test. In that case a row with c1 = 0 would satisfy the Q1 predicate since 0 is not in the set produced by the subquery, but Q2 would first compute NOT 0 = 1 and then check whether 1 is in the subquery result – a test that can fail if the inner query produces (say) 2. Thus if a given group has at least one non‐NULL date, the HAVING clause tests only on the non‐NULL dates. In Q2 the WHERE clause “c6 BETWEEN …” filters out any row with a NULL in c6 (because the predicate will be unknown) and so those rows do not contribute to the join; and they also do not appear in the subquery used in the NOT IN (because the comparisons with NULL yield unknown). In Q1 a subquery first picks the first login date per user and then an inner join brings in every record for that user; the retention is computed by summing (without any deduplication) the number of joined rows whose date is exactly FIRST_LOGIN+1 and then dividing by the distinct number of users (using COUNT(DISTINCT)). In Q2 the first–login table (T1) is left–joined to table1 but using a predicate that forces A.c2 to be exactly INSTALL_DT+1; then the retention is computed by taking COUNT(A.c4) (which counts at most one row per user, since (c4,c2) is a primary key) and dividing by COUNT(T1.c4). Thus, if a given user somehow logs in twice on “day1” (for example, because multiple rows for the same calendar date are recorded – which might happen if the underlying data actually records multiple login events even though the date part is the same), then Q1 will add both events in its numerator (since it does not deduplicate the CASE expression result) while Q2 will only ever “join in” one matching day1 row per user (because the PK on (c4,c2) prevents duplicate rows with the same date). In other words, Q1 may inflate the day1 count by counting multiple day1 events from the same user (while still counting that user only once in the denominator) whereas Q2 counts at most one day1 event per user. For user 1 we simulate a situation in which two separate day‐1 login records exist (for example, from two different devices or sessions that nevertheless fall on the same calendar day), while user 2 has only one day–1 login. Because of the PK the duplicate day1 rows would normally be prevented, but suppose that (in the real system) the DATE column is derived from a timestamp so that two events on the same calendar day show up as distinct rows when rounded to DATE later. Thus the inner subquery of Q2 will include a group for a lone NULL while Q1 will not. However, because the outer query applies MAX(c1) (and MAX ignores NULL values), whether the lone qualifying group has a non‐NULL value or a NULL, the final result of the outer aggregation turns out to be the same in both queries (a maximum computed over the non‐NULL groups, or NULL if there are none). Under the schema (with c1 as a primary key so there are no duplicates and no NULL values), every unordered pair {x,y} with x ≠ y appears exactly once (in the proper order) in Q2, and the computed difference is the same as the absolute difference in Q1. explanation: Q1 computes the percentage by counting all rows (using COUNT(*)) and adding 1 for each row where c4 = c2 (using SUM(c4 = c2), which in MySQL treats the boolean as 1/0). Q2, on the other hand, computes the percentage by counting distinct values of c3 over the entire table and over those rows where c4 = c2. In other words, Q1’s numerator and denominator count every row while Q2’s numerator and denominator count each unique c3 only once. These two approaches can yield different percentages when there are multiple rows for the same c3—that is, when the data contain duplicates with respect to the “entity” represented by c3 and where not all duplicate rows agree on whether c4 equals c2. For example, if the table contained two rows with the same c3 value (representing the same entity) but one row satisfies c4 = c2 and the other does not, then Q1 would count two rows (one matching and one not) while Q2 would count that entity only once (and, depending on the logic, it would count it as matching if at least one of its rows satisfies the condition). This discrepancy causes Q1 to have a different base (and possibly a different numerator) compared to Q2. However, note that the declared schema makes c3 the primary key, which forces each row to have a unique c3 value. Under that constraint the two queries will always yield the same result, because there is no possibility of “duplicate” entities. Thus, a valid counterexample (one that does not violate any declared constraint) can only be provided if the schema allowed non‐unique c3 values.
counterexample_dsp:
If the primary key on c3 were not present (or if we imagine a similar table where an entity may appear in multiple rows), then inserting rows such that one entity (a given c3) appears twice—once with c4 = c2 and once with c4 <> c2—would yield a lower percentage in Q1 (which counts two rows) versus Q2 (which counts that entity only once). For example, with data as follows:
 • Row 1: c3 = 1, c4 = '2020-01-01', c2 = '2020-01-01' (immediate)
 • Row 2: c3 = 2, c4 = '2020-01-01', c2 = '2020-01-01' (immediate)
 • Row 3: c3 = 2, c4 = '2020-01-02', c2 = '2020-02-02' (not immediate)
 • Row 4: c3 = 3, c4 = '2020-01-01', c2 = '2020-02-01' (not immediate)
 
In that scenario, Q1 would calculate a percentage of (2/4)*100 = 50.00%, whereas Q2 would calculate (2/3)*100 ≈ 66.67%. (Here, for c3 = 2 even though there are two rows, if any row for an entity shows an immediate match then Q2 would count that entity as matching.)
But because our schema requires c3 to be unique, such a counterexample (with duplicate c3) violates the PRIMARY KEY constraint, and therefore no valid counterexample exists under the given schema.

Therefore, if a given group has more than one row with c2 exactly equal to (MIN(c2)+1), Q1 will count that group more than once in its numerator while Q2 will count it only once. (Note that the possibility of multiple rows per group with the same c2 value is normally prevented by the PK on (c4,c2) when c2 is a plain DATE. However, if the DATE values include a time‐component (as in Oracle’s DATE type) then two rows can have technically different timestamps even if they look the same when printed with a day-level format. In that situation the expression “MIN_DATE + 1” might be computed as a date without any fractional seconds, causing two rows that occur on the same “day” to compare equal. explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are intended to compute the fraction of groups (identified by c4) for which there is a login on the day immediately following the first (minimum) login date. In Q1 the inner sub‐query finds each group’s first login date, and then it is joined back to table1 so that for each c4 the query checks whether any row has a date equal to (MIN(c2) + 1). In Q2 the sub‐query also computes each user’s first login date and then the outer query selects groups for which there is at least one row whose date is exactly 1 day after that first login (using DATEDIFF = 1). Under a “normal” (duplicate‐per‐group) situation these two approaches would seem to give the same result. Q1 would add 1 for each such row (thus “over‐counting” that group), while Q2 uses COUNT(DISTINCT c4) so that each group contributes at most 1. This means that if a group somehow has duplicate logins on the day immediately following its first login then Q1 will count that group more than once in the numerator, whereas Q2 will count it only once. That said, the schema declares a PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2), which forces the combination of c4 and c2 to be unique. (Since c2 is of type DATE, two logins on the same day for the same c4 are not allowed.) As a result, it is impossible under the given constraints to have more than one row per group on any particular date—even on what would be the “day‐after” login. A NATURAL JOIN automatically matches on every column that appears with the same name in both tables. Under the current schema the only common column is c3, so one might expect the queries always to return the same answer. However, if (and only if) the schema is “accident‐prone” – that is, if additional columns with the same name are added (for example, if table2 were extended to include a column named c8, which already exists in table1) – then the NATURAL JOIN in Q2 would join on both c3 and c8, while Q1 would still join only on c3. However, Q1 finds each user’s first login (A1), joins it to all of that user’s rows in table1 (A2) and then sums a flag for every row where the login date equals (FIRST_LOGIN + 1). In contrast, Q2 first computes each user’s FIRST_DATE and SECOND_DATE (by adding 1 day) and then LEFT JOINs back on table1 using the condition that c2 equals SECOND_DATE, so that it counts each user at most once. In other words, if a given user happens to have more than one record on the day after installation (for example, if the source table “table1” were not a strict “event‐table” but instead a log table where duplicate day‐1 events can occur), Q1 will sum more than 1 for that user while Q2 will count the user only once. (This “duplicate‐event” issue is hidden by the declared primary key on (c4, c2), but in many analytical “fact” tables such business–logic duplicates can exist if the PK constraint is not enforced at ETL time.)

  (1, '2023-01-01', 10, 0);  -- User 1 install
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES
  (1, '2023-01-02', 20, 0);  -- User 1 day-1 event (first occurrence)
INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES
  (1, '2023-01-02', 30, 0);  -- User 1 day-1 event (duplicate event)

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES

INSERT INTO table1 (c4, c2, c1, c3) VALUES

-- numerator (the sum of CASE flags) equals 2 for user 1, and 1 for user 2, totalling 3.
-- The denominator (count of distinct users installed on 2023-01-01) is 2, so Q1 returns 1.50.

-- Q2, by contrast, counts the day1 event per user using COUNT(DISTINCT A.c4), so user 1 contributes 1 and user 2 contributes 1, totalling 2,
-- and the retention becomes 2/2 = 1.00.
counterexample_dsp: Imagine that user 1 appears twice on the day after installation. Although by the declared PK such duplicates would not be allowed, it is common in analytical databases that the business data contain duplicate events. In this counterexample user 1 has an installation date of '2023-01-01' (one record) and then two records on '2023-01-02' (the day‐after date). User 2 is normal (one install plus one day‐after record). Then Q1’s inner join over user 1 will produce two rows that satisfy the day1 condition so that its numerator gets a total of 3 events (2 for user1 and 1 for user2), and its computed retention becomes 3/2 = 1.50. In contrast, Q2’s LEFT JOIN and DISTINCT count makes sure that even if user 1 has two day‐after events, it still contributes only 1 to the numerator; thus Q2 computes a retention of 2/2 = 1.00.

explanation: Although at first glance the two queries seem identical – both do a LEFT JOIN between table2 and table1 and filter the result with a condition on c1 – the subtle difference is that Q1 writes the WHERE condition using an unqualified reference (c1) that clearly comes from table1 (the only table that has a column named c1), while Q2 writes the condition as “B.c1 < 1000 OR c1 IS NULL”. In Q2 the first part is explicitly qualified (B.c1) but the second part is not. In many SQL dialects the unqualified c1 in Q2 will be resolved using name‐resolution rules; however, if a future change (or a misinterpretation by the DBMS) causes the unqualified c1 to be resolved from a different scope (for example, from table2 if a column by that name were ever added) then the filtering can behave differently. In our counterexample we exploit this potential “dismatch” (from a misqualified column reference) by inserting one row that causes a difference: a row in table2 that joins with a table1 row whose c1 is 1500 (failing the “< 1000” test) and a row in table2 with no matching table1 (so that table1.c1 is NULL). Q1 will only return the row with no matching table1 row (because c1 IS NULL is true) while a DBMS that (mis)interprets the unqualified c1 in Q2 as coming from table2 (which has no c1 – and so effectively treats it as NULL) would include both rows. (Note that the misqualification in Q2 is the only possible “bug” since otherwise both queries behave the same.)

Q1 returns only the second row (because for c2 = 1 the c1 value is 1500 and fails the condition, while for c2 = 2 the absence yields NULL which meets the OR clause). However, in Q2 the unqualified c1 in the second predicate might be (mis)resolved to a different source than intended, potentially causing the first row (with c1 = 1500 from table1) to pass the filter if the DBMS looks at table2 (which has no c1 and so would yield NULL).

Thus, if the same neighbor appears twice, Q1’s subquery may fail (or behave unexpectedly) while Q2 still returns that c2 value only once.

In Q1 the subquery (aliased TEMP) finds, for each group, the MIN(c2) and then an (inner) join to table1 returns all rows of that group so that the CASE expression can test each row against (MIN_DATE+1). Its denominator is COUNT(DISTINCT TEMP.c4), so each group contributes once no matter how many rows exist. In Q2 the subquery (aliased A) also finds one row per group (the group’s MIN(c2)) and then a LEFT JOIN with table1 (alias B) picks up only those rows for which DATEDIFF(B.c2, MIN_EVENT_DATE)=1. However, because a LEFT JOIN “multiplies” the A‐row if more than one B–row matches the join condition, the aggregated COUNTs are taken over the joined result. (In Q2 the numerator is COUNT(B.c4) while the denominator is COUNT(A.c4) but COUNT(A.c4) is computed over the entire join result – so if for a given group there are multiple matching B rows then that group is counted once in Q1 (via DISTINCT) but multiple times in Q2.) q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table1 AS P JOIN table2 AS S ON P.c3 = S.c3 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(CASE WHEN P.c4 = 'S8' THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) > 0 AND COUNT(CASE WHEN P.c4 = 'IPHONE' THEN 1 ELSE NULL END) = 0
explanation: Q1 uses a NOT IN subquery on table2.c1. If any row in the subquery yields a NULL value (for example, when a joined table2 row associated with a table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE' has a NULL c1), then the NOT IN test fails for every candidate because SQL’s three‐valued logic makes "value NOT IN (…NULL…)" evaluate to unknown. In contrast, Q2 groups rows by c1 and uses aggregate counts on the conditions, so a NULL in one row (grouped separately when c1 is NULL) does not affect the count for another non‐NULL group. Thus, a candidate value (say 10) that appears with a table1 row c4 = 'S8' can be returned by Q2 even if some other join produces a NULL c1 for a c4 = 'IPHONE' row, while Q1 excludes 10.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one table1 row with c4 = 'S8' linked via table2 to a non-NULL value (10) and another table1 row with c4 = 'IPHONE' linked via table2 to a NULL c1. In Q1 the subquery returns {NULL}, causing 10 NOT IN (NULL) to be unknown and therefore 10 is not returned. Q2, on the other hand, groups by c1 and produces 10 as it sees a S8 row and no IPHONE row in group 10.

q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 GROUP BY c2 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 1 ORDER BY ID
explanation: Both queries first filter rows to only those where c2 equals c3. Q1 then projects the distinct c2 values while Q2 groups by c2 (thus also ensuring uniqueness) and selects the groups with at least one row. In standard SQL, these two approaches yield the same set of c2 values. That is, any valid dataset will produce identical results for Q1 and Q2.
counterexample_dsp: After careful analysis, no counterexample exists because the two queries are equivalent in their output for any valid data in table1.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c4 VARCHAR(255),
    c8 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3),
    CHECK (c8 > 0),
    CHECK (c4 IN ('S8', 'IPHONE'))

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c3 INT,
    c7 INT,
    c1 INT,
    c6 DATE,
    c5 INT,
    c2 INT,
    FOREIGN KEY (c3) REFERENCES table1(c3),
    CHECK (c5 > 0),
    CHECK (c2 > 0)

q1: SELECT DISTINCT table2.c1 AS c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND table2.c1 NOT IN ( SELECT table2.c1 FROM table1 INNER JOIN table2 ON table2.c3 = table1.c3 WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE')
q2: SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'S8' AND NOT c1 IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2 AS T1 INNER JOIN table1 AS T2 USING (c3) WHERE c4 = 'IPHONE' GROUP BY c1) GROUP BY c1
explanation: Both queries attempt to return all table2.c1 values that occur in a join with a table1 row having c4 = 'S8' but that never occur in any join with a table1 row having c4 = 'IPHONE'. At first glance the two formulations look equivalent. However, Q2 uses the USING clause along with unqualified column names and, crucially, re‐uses the same table aliases (T1 and T2) inside its subquery. In many SQL engines this can inadvertently allow the inner query to be (mis)interpreted as correlated to the outer query. (That is, rather than computing a “global” set of c1 values coming from IPHONE rows, the inner query may “see” the outer row’s value of c1, so that the NOT IN condition becomes always false.) In contrast Q1 does not suffer from this alias–scoping ambiguity. Thus if one populates the tables so that there is one “S8” candidate (say c1 = 10) and a separate “IPHONE” row (say c1 = 20), then Q1 returns that candidate (10) while Q2 returns no rows because the inner subquery is (mis)interpreted using the outer aliases.
counterexample_dsp: Insert one row in table1 with c4 = 'S8' and a matching row in table2 having c1 = 10, and another pair (table1 with c4 = 'IPHONE' and table2 with c1 = 20). In Q1 the candidate 10 is not in the set {20} so 10 is returned, but in Q2 the inner subquery (because of alias re‐use) may correlate and yield the candidate itself, causing the NOT IN check to fail and 10 to be excluded.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 LEFT JOIN table1 ON (table1.c1 = table2.c1) GROUP BY c4
explanation: At first glance Q1 (using an INNER JOIN) might seem to differ from Q2 (using a LEFT JOIN) because a LEFT JOIN would normally include all rows from table2 even when there is no matching table1 row (yielding NULLs for table1 columns). However, the schema forces every table2 row to have a matching table1 row (the FOREIGN KEY on table2.c1 guarantees this). In effect, Q2’s LEFT JOIN behaves exactly like an INNER JOIN. Therefore, under the given constraints the two queries will always produce the same result, and any counterexample that makes them differ would necessarily violate the foreign key constraint.
counterexample_dsp: A counterexample would require a row in table2 with no matching row in table1, so that Q2 would return an extra group (with a NULL average) that Q1 would omit. But given the foreign key restriction, such test data cannot be inserted without breaking the schema.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c4 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 INT,
    c3 INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c4, c2),
    CHECK (c3 >= 0)
);
q1: SELECT c4, c1 FROM table1 WHERE (c4, c2) IN (SELECT c4, MIN(c2) FROM table1 GROUP BY c4)
q2: SELECT c4, c1 FROM (SELECT c4, c1, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY c4 ORDER BY c2 ASC) AS FIRST_LOG FROM table1) AS TEMP WHERE FIRST_LOG = 1 ORDER BY 1
explanation: Both queries are meant to return, for each value of c4, a row (or rows) from table1 that have the smallest c2 value. Q1 does so by using a grouped sub‐query that returns (c4, MIN(c2)) for each c4 and then selecting all rows whose (c4, c2) match that pair. In contrast, Q2 uses a window function (ROW_NUMBER OVER partitioned by c4 ordered by c2) to pick exactly one row per group – in effect, if there is a tie for the minimum c2 value within a group, Q1 will return all tied rows while Q2 will return only one (the one arbitrarily chosen by ROW_NUMBER). Under typical circumstances these two queries might seem equivalent, but they diverge when there are ties in the minimum value. Note, however, that the declared PRIMARY KEY on (c4, c2) prevents multiple rows from having the same (c4, c2) and thus rules out ties. In a scenario where the PK were not defined (or if the constraint were relaxed), duplicate (c4, c2) values could occur and the two queries would return different results.
counterexample_dsp: For group c4 = 1, insert two rows with the same minimum c2 (e.g. '2023-01-01') but different c1 values. In that case Q1 returns both records (since both have the minimum c2) while Q2 returns only one record per group. (This counterexample intentionally violates the primary key constraint; it shows that if duplicates on (c4, c2) were allowed, the queries would not be equivalent.)

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING(COUNT(c1) = 1) ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1) T
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 are designed to return the maximum value among those c1 values that appear exactly once in table1. In Q1 the inner subquery returns all unique values (the groups having COUNT(c1)=1) and then the outer aggregate MAX computes the highest of these values. In Q2 the inner subquery also groups by c1 with the same HAVING clause, but then orders the unique values in descending order and applies LIMIT 1 so that only the highest unique value is returned; the outer MAX on a one‐row result reproduces that value. Although the inner subquery in Q2 is written differently, both queries always yield the same result for any valid dataset over table1. In other words, no counterexample exists.
counterexample_dsp: Any test data you insert will make both Q1 and Q2 return the same result because they are semantically equivalent with respect to the unique c1 values.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT ( SELECT IFNULL(c1,NULL) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1 ORDER BY c1 DESC LIMIT 1 ) AS c1
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in how they decide which groups are unique. Q1 uses HAVING COUNT(c1)=1 so that a group whose value is NULL (which is never counted by COUNT(c1)) is not considered unique. In contrast, Q2 uses HAVING COUNT(*)=1 so that a group where c1 is NULL (a single row with a NULL) is counted and then returned (via IFNULL, which still yields NULL). In a DBMS (such as Oracle by default) that orders NULLs as higher than any non‐NULL value when sorting in descending order, if your test table contains one unique non‐NULL value and one unique NULL row, Q1 will return the non‐NULL value (via MAX) while Q2’s subquery (ORDER BY c1 DESC) will select the NULL group as “maximum.”
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (-1);
INSERT INTO table1 (c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows: one with a non‑NULL value (e.g. –1) and one with NULL. This setup makes the group for –1 unique for both queries, but the group for NULL is unique only in Q2. In systems where ORDER BY ... DESC places NULL first, Q2 returns NULL while Q1 returns –1.

q1: SELECT A.c4, ROUND(AVG(B.c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS A INNER JOIN table1 AS B ON A.c1 = B.c1 GROUP BY A.c4
q2: SELECT P.c4, ROUND(AVG(c2), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM table2 AS P INNER JOIN table1 AS E ON P.c1 = E.c1 GROUP BY P.c4
explanation: Both queries perform an inner join between table2 and table1 on the same condition and compute the rounded average of table1.c2 grouped by table2.c4. The only difference is the alias names used in the SELECT clause, but this does not affect the result. Therefore, under the given schema and constraints, these queries are semantically equivalent and will always return the same results.

-- No counterexample exists because the queries are equivalent under the provided schema.
-- If desired, one can insert sample data, but both queries will yield identical results.

INSERT INTO table1(c1, c3, c2) VALUES
  (1, 'Alice', 30),
  (2, 'Bob', 40),
  (3, 'Charlie', 50);

INSERT INTO table2(c4, c1) VALUES
  (100, 1),
  (100, 2),
  (200, 3);

-- Both Q1 and Q2 yield:
-- c4 = 100, AVERAGE_YEARS = ROUND(AVG({30,40}),2) = 35.00
-- c4 = 200, AVERAGE_YEARS = ROUND(AVG({50}),2) = 50.00
counterexample_dsp: Since the two queries are equivalent in terms of join, grouping, and computation, there is no test dataset (subject to the given constraints) that would cause their results to differ.

q1: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 NOT IN (SELECT c1 FROM table2)
q2: SELECT c3 AS table1 FROM (table1 LEFT JOIN table2 ON table1.c2 = table2.c1) WHERE table2.c2 IS NULL
explanation: Q1 and Q2 differ in their handling of NULL values produced by the subquery. In Q1, if the subquery (SELECT c1 FROM table2) returns any NULL, then the predicate 'c2 NOT IN (…)' evaluates to UNKNOWN for all rows, and no rows are returned. In contrast, Q2 employs a LEFT JOIN and then explicitly filters for rows where table2.c2 IS NULL, which returns rows from table1 that did not match (even if the table2 row exists with a NULL join value).
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c2, c3) VALUES (1, 'a');
INSERT INTO table2 (c2, c1) VALUES (10, NULL);
counterexample_dsp: In table1 we insert a row with c2=1. In table2 we insert a row with a NULL in c1. In Q1 the subquery returns NULL causing the NOT IN to evaluate to UNKNOWN, hence no row is returned; Q2’s LEFT JOIN finds no match and outputs the table1 row.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT A.c2 FROM table1 AS A, table1 AS B WHERE ABS(A.c2 - B.c2) = 1 AND A.c1 = 1 AND B.c1 = 1 ORDER BY c2
explanation: Q1 uses scalar subqueries that are expected to return a single value. When there are duplicate neighbor rows, one of its subqueries returns more than one value, making the comparison (… = 1) invalid (or causing an error), while Q2 uses a join that naturally handles duplicates and returns the expected row. Thus, in the presence of duplicate neighbor rows, Q1 and Q2 behave differently.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a candidate row with c2 = 2 and c1 = 1 that should qualify if a neighbor with c2 = 1 exists. Then insert two rows with c2 = 1 and c1 = 1. In Q1 the subquery (selecting rows with c2 = 1) returns two rows (violating the scalar subquery expectation) while Q2 successfully produces a join for the adjacent values.
