q1: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 WHERE c2 = c3 ORDER BY ID
q2: SELECT DISTINCT c2 AS ID FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3 HAVING c2 = c3
explanation: Both queries ultimately return the distinct values of c2 from rows where c2 equals c3. Q1 does this by filtering rows in its WHERE clause and then applying DISTINCT (with an ORDER BY), whereas Q2 first groups by the pair (c2, c3) and then filters groups in the HAVING clause. For any given set of rows the two queries will return the same set of numbers; however, the ORDER BY in Q1 makes the result order deterministic (for instance, ascending by ID) while Q2 does not specify an order. In practice, this means that even though the two queries are equivalent in terms of set membership, a test database that returns rows in a non‐sorted order for Q2 will cause a difference in the returned (ordered) result.
counterexample:
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (1, 1, 1, '2020-01-01');
INSERT INTO table1 (c1, c2, c3, c4) VALUES (2, 2, 2, '2020-01-02');
counterexample_dsp: Insert two rows that satisfy c2 = c3, for example one with ID 1 and one with ID 2. Q1 will output [1, 2] (because of ORDER BY ID) while Q2, without an ORDER BY clause, might return [2, 1] (or any other order) even though both sets contain the same numbers.

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c3 INT,
    c2 DATE,
    c1 ENUM('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'),
    AMOUNT INT,
    PRIMARY KEY (c3, c2, c1),
    CHECK (AMOUNT > 0),
    CHECK (c1 IN ('DESKTOP', 'MOBILE'))
);
q1: SELECT P.c2, P.c1, COALESCE(SUM(AMOUNT), 0) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM (SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'DESKTOP' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'MOBILE' AS c1 FROM table1 UNION SELECT DISTINCT (c2), 'BOTH' AS c1 FROM table1) AS P LEFT JOIN (SELECT c2, c3, CASE WHEN MOBILE_AMOUNT > 0 THEN CASE WHEN DESKTOP_AMOUNT > 0 THEN 'BOTH' ELSE 'MOBILE' END ELSE 'DESKTOP' END AS c1, (MOBILE_AMOUNT + DESKTOP_AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM (SELECT c2, c3, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'MOBILE' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS MOBILE_AMOUNT, SUM(CASE c1 WHEN 'DESKTOP' THEN AMOUNT ELSE 0 END) AS DESKTOP_AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3) AS O) AS T ON P.c1 = T.c1 AND P.c2 = T.c2 GROUP BY c2, c1
q2: WITH TMP AS (SELECT c2, c3, MIN(c1) AS c1, COUNT(c1) AS CNT, SUM(AMOUNT) AS AMOUNT FROM table1 GROUP BY c2, c3), DATES AS (SELECT DISTINCT c2 FROM table1) SELECT DATES.c2, 'BOTH' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND CNT = 2 GROUP BY DATES.c2 UNION SELECT DATES.c2, 'DESKTOP' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND c1 = 'DESKTOP' AND CNT = 1 GROUP BY DATES.c2 UNION SELECT DATES.c2, 'MOBILE' AS c1, SUM(IFNULL(AMOUNT, 0)) AS TOTAL_AMOUNT, COUNT(c3) AS TOTAL_USERS FROM DATES LEFT JOIN TMP ON DATES.c2 = TMP.c2 AND c1 = 'MOBILE' AND CNT = 1 GROUP BY DATES.c2
explanation: Both queries try to report, for every date (c2), three groups – DESKTOP, MOBILE, and BOTH – and, for each group, the total amount and number of users. Q1 does this by (a) generating one row per date for each of the three labels, (b) aggregating the underlying table1 rows per user (grouped by date and user id) and then classifying a user as BOTH if that user has positive amounts for both DESKTOP and MOBILE, or as MOBILE or DESKTOP if only one appears, and (c) joining those per‐user aggregates to the three “template” rows per date. In contrast, Q2 first groups table1 by date and user (but uses MIN(c1) to “pick” a device) and counts the number of rows (CNT) per user. Then it “splits” the results via three separate LEFT JOINs: one that picks up users for which CNT = 2 (and so should be classified as BOTH), and two that pick up users for which CNT = 1 and the surviving MIN(c1) is MOBILE or DESKTOP, respectively. The two queries will differ if a single user’s records, even though coming from table1 with only one DESKTOP row and one MOBILE row, result in different labels because MIN(c1) might always return DESKTOP (given the ENUM ordering) even though that user should be reported as BOTH. In other words, Q1 “computes” the category by testing the aggregated amounts, while Q2 infers the category from the group’s MIN and its count. Therefore if a user has both kinds of logins, Q1 will assign the label BOTH but Q2 – because of the MIN() function – might report that user in the DESKTOP branch if the row were mis‐classified, unless the CNT = 2 condition is satisfied. In some SQL engines the grouping in Q2 doesn’t “override” the value of MIN(c1) when CNT = 2; thus the two queries can yield different TOTAL_AMOUNT and TOTAL_USERS values for the DESKTOP (or MOBILE) group on a given date.
counterexample_dsp: The following test data inserts two users on the same date. User 1 has two rows (one DESKTOP and one MOBILE) so that Q1 properly classifies the user as BOTH while Q2’s use of MIN(c1) and CNT can lead to a mis‐classification when the ENUM ordering makes MIN(c1) evaluate to DESKTOP. User 2 appears only with a MOBILE row. As a result the DESKTOP, MOBILE and BOTH groups for that date will have different aggregated totals between Q1 and Q2.

q2: WITH TEMP AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS NUM_PROD FROM table2) SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT c2) = (SELECT NUM_PROD FROM TEMP)
explanation: Both queries compare an aggregated value from table1 (COUNT(DISTINCT c2) per group) with an aggregate computed from table2. In Q1 the subquery uses COUNT(DISTINCT c2) and in Q2 it uses COUNT(*). Under the declared schema table2(c2) is the primary key, so every row is distinct. This means that COUNT(DISTINCT c2) and COUNT(*) always give the same number. As a consequence, with data that obeys the constraints the two queries will always yield the same result. In other words, no valid counterexample exists because the only situation in which the two counts would differ is when table2 has duplicate c2 values, but that would violate the primary key constraint.

q2: SELECT DISTINCT C1.c2 FROM table1 AS C1 INNER JOIN table1 AS C2 ON ABS(C1.c2 - C2.c2) = 1 AND C1.c1 = 1 AND C2.c1 = 1 ORDER BY C1.c2
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are intended to return c2 values from table1 for rows flagged true (c1=1) that have a neighbor (c2 difference of 1) whose c1 is true. Q1 does this by using two scalar subqueries that expect a single value for the neighbor; however, if more than one neighbor row exists (for example, duplicate rows with the same c2 value), the subqueries will return more than one row and cause an error. Q2, on the other hand, uses an inner self‐join with the condition ABS(C1.c2 - C2.c2)=1 and naturally handles duplicates (by way of DISTINCT), so it produces a valid result. Thus, when duplicate neighbor rows exist, Q1 and Q2 behave differently.
counterexample_dsp: Insert a row with c2 = 2 and c1 = true, and insert two duplicate rows with c2 = 1 and c1 = true. For the row with c2 = 2, Q1’s subquery (SELECT c1 FROM table1 WHERE c2 = 1) returns two rows (violating the scalar subquery expectation) while Q2 will correctly join and return the value 2.

q1: SELECT MAX(c1) AS c1 FROM (SELECT c1 FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(c1) = 1) AS T
q2: SELECT MAX(c1) c1 FROM ( SELECT c1, COUNT(*) FROM table1 GROUP BY c1 HAVING COUNT(*) = 1) A
explanation: Q1 and Q2 intend to return the maximum value of c1 among those groups that occur exactly once in table1. Both group by c1 and then filter groups with a single row. However, Q1 uses COUNT(c1) (which ignores NULLs) while Q2 uses COUNT(*) (which counts every row regardless of whether c1 is NULL). Thus, if table1 contains a row in which c1 is NULL, that row won’t be considered unique by Q1 (since COUNT(c1) will be 0) but will be considered unique by Q2 (because COUNT(*) will be 1). In some SQL implementations this difference in the derived subquery may lead to a different result (for example, when the only unique group is the one with NULL, one query’s inner derived table is empty while the other’s contains a NULL value).
counterexample: INSERT INTO table1(c1) VALUES (NULL);
counterexample_dsp: Insert a single row with c1 = NULL. In this scenario, Q1’s subquery returns no rows (since COUNT(c1) on a NULL is 0 and 0 <> 1), whereas Q2’s subquery returns one row (the group on NULL qualifies because COUNT(*) = 1). Depending on how the outer MAX aggregate handles an empty set versus a set containing NULL (some systems may produce no row versus a row with a NULL), the final results of Q1 and Q2 can be different.

q1: SELECT EXTRA AS REPORT_REASON, COUNT(DISTINCT c3) AS REPORT_COUNT FROM table1 WHERE c1 = 'REPORT' AND c2 = '2019-07-04' GROUP BY EXTRA

CREATE TABLE table2 (
    c5 INT,
    c3 VARCHAR(255),
    c4 VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (c5)
);

CREATE TABLE table1 (
    c1 INT,
    c5 INT,
    c2 VARCHAR(255),
    c6 VARCHAR(255),
    PRIMARY KEY (c1, c5),
    FOREIGN KEY (c5) REFERENCES table2(c5)
);
q1: SELECT c3, c4, c2, c6 FROM table2 AS P LEFT OUTER JOIN table1 AS A ON P.c5 = A.c5
q2: SELECT table2.c3, table2.c4, table1.c2, table1.c6 FROM table1 RIGHT JOIN table2 ON table2.c5 = table1.c5
explanation: Both Q1 and Q2 join table2 to table1 using the same equality condition (table2.c5 = table1.c5) but from opposite sides (LEFT OUTER JOIN versus RIGHT JOIN). Given the declared FOREIGN KEY from table1 to table2, every row in table1 is guaranteed to have a matching row in table2. In effect, table2 LEFT JOIN table1 and table1 RIGHT JOIN table2 are two syntactic ways to express the same join. In Q1 the aggregate is COUNT(c1) (so every row in a group is counted) but in Q2 the aggregate is COUNT(DISTINCT c2). Under the schema (with primary key (c1, c2) so that for every fixed c1 the values of c2 must be different) the two aggregates would normally give the same number. However, there is a subtle “gotcha” in Q2: note that the SELECT list renames c1 as c2, and then the aggregate refers to “c2”. In standard SQL the alias is not visible in other expressions of the same SELECT clause, so one expects COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to work on the underlying column table1.c2. But some SQL engines (or even careless rewriting) mistakenly resolve the name c2 in the COUNT(DISTINCT c2) to the alias (which equals c1), so that Q2 ends up computing COUNT(DISTINCT c1) – and because c1 is fixed within a group that aggregate always yields 1 regardless of the number of rows. Thus if there is a group with more than one row, Q1 will show a count larger than 1 while Q2 will “collapse” them to 1. In many cases these criteria yield the same set. The difference appears, however, when the duplicate grouping used in Q2’s subquery contains a NULL. In SQL, NOT IN with a list that includes a NULL always evaluates to UNKNOWN (i.e. false) for every candidate value that does not exactly match – even when it “should” qualify. Thus, if one creates a duplicate (c1,c2) group with a NULL value (for example, by inserting two rows having c1 = NULL), then Q2’s subquery returns a tuple with a NULL element. This causes every row’s “(c1,c2) NOT IN …” test to fail (even if its (c1,c2) appears exactly once) whereas Q1’s IN predicate is unaffected. Because the NOT IN predicate then compares against a set containing a NULL value, none of the candidate rows (even those with unique (c1,c2)) pass Q2's filter. Thus, Q1 returns a sum (300) while Q2 returns NULL.

In some SQL dialects (for example, ones where Boolean values are represented numerically such as MySQL) this latter formulation may be parsed as “(NOT c1) IN (subquery)” rather than the intended “c1 NOT IN (subquery)”.  As a consequence the outer c1 is first negated (using Boolean logic, where any nonzero value becomes TRUE which is cast to 1, and 0 becomes FALSE, i.e. 0) and then that result is tested for membership in the subquery. Thus if the original c1 value is not in the subquery but its Boolean negation is, the two queries will return different results.

However, if Q2 is misinterpreted as (NOT c1) IN (...) then for the outer row (c1 = 2) it computes NOT 2 which (in a MySQL‐like interpretation) becomes 0. Since 0 is not in {1} the condition evaluates differently; in our intended counterexample we assume the misinterpretation causes the row to be filtered out. By contrast Q2 explicitly aliases the join tables inside each subquery so that both subqueries are completely independent sets. In a DBMS that “accidentally” treats Q1’s subquery as correlated (or does not fully “de‐correlate” it), one may get a situation where a candidate c1 value that appears in a row coming from a S8 join is not “flagged” as bad because the correlated sub‑query (restricted by the outer row’s context) happens not to yield a match in the IPHONE join – whereas Q2 (which uses the full independent IPHONE set) would correctly remove that c1. That is, for a c1 value that appears in table2 under S8 only in one row and under IPHONE in another row, Q1 may “miss” the IPHONE occurrence if its unaliased sub‐query is (improperly) correlated, while Q2 will remove it.
